subject: Physics
chapter: Chapter 2: Motion in a Straight Line
central_question: How can one describe, interpret and predict the motion of an object along a straight line using velocity, acceleration, graphs and kinematic relations?
in_scope_units: 2.1 Introduction — motion, rectilinear motion, point-object approximation and the scope of kinematics.
2.2 Instantaneous velocity and speed — limiting definition of velocity, slope of the position–time graph and speed as the magnitude of velocity.
2.3 Acceleration — average and instantaneous acceleration, signs of velocity and acceleration, and interpretation of x–t and v–t graphs.
2.4 Kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion — graphical and calculus forms relating displacement, velocity, acceleration and time.
Applications in the source — vertical motion, free fall, Galileo’s odd-number law, stopping distance and reaction time.
Relative velocity — listed in the chapter contents and represented in the end exercise on the police van, bullet and thief’s car.
banned_topics: Detailed causes of motion and force laws

known_pitfalls.claim: A negative acceleration always means an object is slowing down.
known_pitfalls.correction: The sign of acceleration depends on the chosen positive direction; speed decreases only when acceleration is opposite to velocity.

known_pitfalls.claim: Zero velocity at an instant means zero acceleration.
known_pitfalls.correction: A vertically thrown particle has zero velocity at its highest point while its acceleration due to gravity remains non-zero.

known_pitfalls.claim: The kinematic equations are valid for any one-dimensional motion.
known_pitfalls.correction: The standard equations v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) require constant acceleration.

recommended_example_progression: NCERT Example 2.1 — obtain instantaneous and average velocity from x = a + bt².
NCERT Example 2.2 — derive the constant-acceleration equations using calculus.
NCERT Example 2.3 — analyse a ball thrown upward from a building.
NCERT Example 2.6 — derive stopping distance and its dependence on initial speed.
NCERT Exercise 2.14 — apply relative velocity to the police-van and thief-car situation.
